promptText: What specific problem did QLoRA (2023) solve that plain LoRA (2021) did not?
options: QLoRA eliminated the need for any GPU during training

QLoRA reduced the memory required to hold the frozen base model during training (via 4-bit quantization), whereas LoRA had already reduced only the trainable parameter memory, leaving the base model's full 16-bit footprint as the remaining bottleneck
QLoRA introduced the low-rank B·A adapter concept for the first time
QLoRA removed the need for a calibration or training dataset entirely
explanation: LoRA shrank trainable-parameter memory, but the frozen base model still had to fit in GPU memory at 16-bit; QLoRA attacked that remaining wall by quantizing the frozen base to 4-bit.

promptText: In LoRA, what does the expression W + B·A represent?
options: A completely new weight matrix that replaces W with random values
The effective weight used at inference: the original frozen weight W plus a low-rank correction formed by multiplying two small trainable matrices B and A
A quantization formula converting W from FP32 to INT4
The gradient update applied directly to W during full fine-tuning
explanation: W stays frozen; the adaptation is expressed entirely as the low-rank product B·A added on top, which is what gets trained.

promptText: Why does full fine-tuning have a higher theoretical quality ceiling than LoRA, but also a higher catastrophic-forgetting risk?
options: Full fine-tuning uses a different loss function that is inherently more accurate

Full fine-tuning allows gradient descent to move every weight in any direction the loss landscape suggests with no constraint, while LoRA's low-rank structure mechanically limits how far the effective weights can drift from their pretrained values
Full fine-tuning always trains for more epochs than LoRA by default
LoRA cannot access the model's attention layers, which limits both its ceiling and its forgetting risk equally
explanation: LoRA's rank constraint acts as an implicit regularizer, structurally limiting available update directions independent of how aggressively you train.

promptText: What does the 'intrinsic dimensionality' argument claim as theoretical justification for why LoRA works despite training far fewer parameters?
options: That the base model's entire weight matrix is fundamentally low-rank and therefore less expressive than believed

That although a weight matrix has enormous capacity, the actual update needed to adapt an already-general model to a narrower task tends to live in a much lower-dimensional subspace than the full matrix, even though the base weights themselves remain full-rank
That LoRA only works on tasks involving fewer than 16 output classes
That gradient descent inherently produces low-rank updates for any neural network, regardless of task
explanation: The claim is about the update needed for adaptation, not about the base model's own expressiveness, which remains full-rank and general.

promptText: What is the fundamental serving-architecture tradeoff between merging a LoRA adapter into the base model versus keeping it separate?
options: Merging always improves model accuracy; keeping separate always degrades it

Merging produces a single artifact with inference identical in speed/shape to an ordinary model but loses the ability to cheaply hot-swap or subtract the adaptation; keeping adapters separate enables one shared base model to serve many tenants/variants at the cost of a small per-request B·A computation and added serving complexity
Merging requires quantization while keeping separate does not
Keeping adapters separate is always cheaper in every dimension, so merging is never justified
explanation: This is a serving-architecture decision, not a training-time one: merge for simplicity and latency, keep separate for multi-tenant flexibility.

promptText: What happens if the LoRA rank r is set too low for the task's actual complexity, and what is the correct fix?
options: Training becomes numerically unstable and immediately diverges; the fix is to lower the learning rate

Training loss plateaus at a level higher than a full fine-tune would achieve, because the low-rank subspace cannot express the needed update; the fix is a higher rank or broader set of adapted layers, not more training epochs
The model automatically falls back to full fine-tuning to compensate
Nothing changes since rank has no effect on achievable training loss
explanation: The bottleneck is expressiveness, not optimization difficulty, so more epochs risks overfitting the constrained subspace rather than fixing the plateau.

promptText: QLoRA depends on three specific load-bearing ideas beyond generic 4-bit quantization. What does NF4 (4-bit NormalFloat) specifically address that a naive uniform 4-bit scheme would not?
options: NF4 removes the need for a frozen base model entirely

Pretrained weights cluster tightly around zero in an approximately normal distribution rather than being uniform; NF4 spaces its 16 representable values to match a normal distribution's quantiles, so more precision budget falls where weights are actually dense
NF4 compresses the LoRA adapter matrices, not the base model
NF4 is a training algorithm that replaces Adam as the optimizer
explanation: A uniform 4-bit scheme wastes representable values on sparse tails; NF4 matches the actual bell-curve distribution of weights, preserving more quality at the same bit width.

promptText: Why is 'we used QLoRA' not a valid privacy mitigation for training-data memorization concerns?
options: QLoRA cannot be used with sensitive data at all, so the question is moot

Quantizing the frozen base model's storage precision has no bearing on what the trainable adapter matrices themselves may have memorized from the fine-tuning examples; the adapter carries the same memorization risk as a full-precision LoRA adapter trained on the same data
QLoRA automatically encrypts all training data before use
QLoRA deletes the training dataset immediately after each epoch
explanation: 4-bit storage of the frozen base has nothing to do with what the trainable adapter learned; memorization risk is unchanged from a full-precision LoRA run on the same data.

promptText: Structurally, why is prompt/prefix-tuning's forgetting failure mode categorically milder than LoRA's or full fine-tuning's?
options: Prompt-tuning uses a smaller learning rate than the other methods

Because the base model's weights are mathematically untouched in prompt/prefix-tuning, any quality loss can only come from the learned prefix crowding out or conflicting with the base model's default behavior, not from the base weights themselves being damaged, which is structurally possible in full fine-tuning and LoRA
Prompt-tuning is immune to catastrophic forgetting because it does not use gradient descent at all
Prefix-tuning only operates on the output layer, which cannot cause forgetting by definition
explanation: Since base weights are never touched, damage of the kind that harms the base model's own weights is structurally impossible; any degradation is a milder, input-level conflict.

promptText: What is the recommended progression for choosing which layers to adapt with LoRA, per the chapter's staged approach?
options: Always adapt every layer in the model from the very first training run to maximize quality

Start with just query and value attention projections; expand to all attention projections (Q, K, V, O) if quality plateaus; add feed-forward layers only for demanding tasks after attention-only adaptation has been tried and demonstrably falls short
Start with the feed-forward layers since they are the largest and most important
Randomly select a different subset of layers on each training run and average the results
explanation: This staged escalation avoids the cost of adapting the largest matrices (feed-forward) until attention-only adaptation has been demonstrated insufficient on held-out evaluation.

promptText: What is the consequence of an implementation bug where a LoRA/QLoRA setup fails to actually set the base model's parameters to non-trainable (requires_grad = False)?
options: Nothing changes since LoRA adapters override gradient computation automatically

It silently turns a cheap LoRA/QLoRA run into an accidental, extremely expensive full fine-tune, with unused adapter matrices along for the ride — a real, reported failure mode, not a hypothetical one
The training job immediately crashes with an out-of-memory error, making the bug easy to catch
It has no effect on cost, only on final model quality
explanation: This is why sanity-checking trainable-parameter count against the expected order of magnitude before a long unattended training run is a recommended best practice.

promptText: For full fine-tuning with mixed precision and Adam, the chapter estimates roughly 16 bytes of memory per parameter (2 bytes weights + 2 bytes gradients + 8 bytes optimizer state + 4 bytes master weights). Why does LoRA reduce this to roughly 2 bytes per parameter for the base model, with only negligible additional memory for the adapter?
options: LoRA quantizes every weight to 2 bits, which happens to average to 2 bytes across the whole model

Because the base model's weights are frozen and receive no gradients or optimizer state at all, LoRA only needs to store the base weights themselves (bf16, 2 bytes/param) plus tiny adapter matrices and their gradients/optimizer state, which are a negligible fraction of total parameter count
LoRA uses FP8 precision for gradients, which is exactly one-eighth the size of FP32 optimizer state
LoRA does not require an optimizer at all, since B and A are updated using a fixed rule rather than gradient descent
explanation: Freezing the base model eliminates gradient and optimizer-state memory for it entirely; only the adapter's tiny parameter count needs the full gradient/optimizer treatment.

promptText: The chapter gives the LoRA parameter reduction factor as approximately d / (2r) for a square d×d weight matrix. What does this formula imply about the relationship between rank and parameter savings, and why does this matter when tuning rank upward to fix a quality plateau?
options: The reduction factor is independent of r, so raising rank has no cost implication at all

Doubling the rank r halves the reduction factor, meaning parameter savings shrink as expressiveness increases — so raising rank to fix a quality ceiling is a real, non-free tradeoff between adapter capacity and the savings that make LoRA attractive in the first place, not a value to maximize by default
The formula shows that reduction factor increases as rank increases, so higher rank is always more memory-efficient
The formula only applies to feed-forward layers, not attention projections
explanation: Rank is a deliberate knob trading expressiveness for parameter savings; the inverse relationship in d/(2r) means raising it to fix a plateau has a real, quantifiable cost.

promptText: Why might a regulated organization with right-to-deletion obligations deliberately choose to keep LoRA adapters separate from the base model even when merging would otherwise be the simpler serving choice?
options: Regulations legally prohibit the use of low-rank matrices in any production system

Once an adapter is merged into base weights, there is no clean way to 'remove' a specific tenant's or dataset's contribution short of retraining from the pre-merge checkpoint; keeping adapters separate preserves the ability to audit or revoke a specific adaptation on demand
Merged models are always slower to serve than models with separate adapters
Separate adapters are required by law to be stored in a different country than the base model
explanation: Merging is mechanically irreversible without a kept pre-merge copy, which conflicts with data-subject-erasure obligations that separate adapters can satisfy more cleanly.

promptText: Which point on the PEFT spectrum is most appropriate when a platform needs many cheap, swappable task or tenant variants served off one shared frozen deployment, with training budget very tight?
options: Full fine-tuning, because maximum degrees of freedom guarantees the best fit for every variant

Prefix/prompt-tuning or LoRA/QLoRA kept unmerged, since both leave the shared base model reusable across variants, with prefix/prompt-tuning representing the minimum-footprint end of that spectrum, most suited when training budget is extremely tight and the base model is large enough to support it well
QLoRA merged into the base model for every tenant, producing one deployable artifact per tenant
There is no PEFT approach suited to this use case; a bespoke fully custom architecture is required
explanation: Prompt/prefix-tuning trains even fewer parameters than LoRA and never touches base weights, making it the natural fit for many cheap, swappable variants on one frozen deployment.
